title: Text, numbers, dates and TRUE/FALSE
summary: How Excel decides what you typed, and why some numbers end up as text.
objectives: Recognise text, numbers, dates and TRUE/FALSE by how they line up.
Type dates the way Excel understands them.
Keep IDs with leading zeros as text.
Turn numbers stored as text back into numbers.

lecture.title: How Excel decides what you typed

p: Every entry becomes one of four kinds: **text**, a **number**, a **date** (which is secretly a number) or a **logical** value, TRUE or FALSE.
You can tell them apart at a glance: text lines up on the **left**, numbers and dates on the **right**, TRUE and FALSE in the **centre**. That alignment is Excel telling you what it thinks you typed.

visual.caption: Text left, numbers and dates right, TRUE/FALSE centred

p: Excel counts days from 1 January 1900. **15-08-2026** is really day 46,249 with a date format on top. That’s why you can subtract one date from another to get the days between them.
In India, Excel expects **day first**: type `15-08-2026`, `15/8/26` or `15-Aug-2026`. If a date stays on the left, Excel didn’t recognise it and stored text instead.

check.q: You type a date and it lines up on the **left** of the cell. What does that tell you?
options: Excel stored it as text, not a date
check.explain: Real dates are numbers, so they line up on the right. Left means text.

why.0: Real dates line up on the right, like numbers.
why.2: A narrow column shows ##### for dates, not left alignment.

lecture.title: When numbers end up as text

p: Excel treats `007` as the number 7 and drops the zeros. For IDs, PIN codes with zeros or roll numbers like **0042**, start with an apostrophe: `'0042`. The apostrophe doesn’t show; it tells Excel “keep this as text”.
Excel keeps only **15 significant digits**. A 16-digit card number loses its last digit. Store long IDs as text; you never do maths on them anyway.

bad.title: Typed 0042
bad.text: Excel stores 42. The zeros are gone for good.

good.title: Typed '0042
good.text: Excel stores the text 0042, exactly as written.

p: Data copied from websites or exported from software often arrives as text that only looks like numbers. Clues: it sits on the **left**, a small **green triangle** marks the corner, and **SUM ignores it**, so totals come out wrong.
Fix: select the cells, click the warning sign and choose **Convert to Number**. Or retype them. In this app, right-click and choose Convert to number.

visual.caption: Green triangles flag numbers stored as text; Convert to Number fixes them

check.q: A column of amounts adds up to 0 with =SUM. Each amount sits on the left with a green triangle. What’s wrong?
options: The amounts are stored as text
check.explain: SUM skips text. Convert the cells to numbers and the total appears.

demo.intro: Watch what happens to each kind of entry as it’s typed.

steps.say: Text lines up on the left.
A number lines up on the right. The comma is just formatting.
Day first, and Excel recognises a date: it lines up on the right.
TRUE is a logical value. It sits in the centre.
007 becomes the number 7. The zeros are lost.
With an apostrophe in front, the zeros stay: it’s text now.

demo.outro: Left, right, centre: the alignment always tells you what Excel stored.

lab.intro: Fill in the joining form so every value is stored as the right kind, then fix the expense claims that arrived as text.

tasks.prompt: In **B3**, type her monthly salary: **52,000**. It should be a real number.
hints: A real number lines up on the right.
Don’t type ₹ with a space or Rs. after it.

mistakes.msg: That went in as text. Type just the digits, like 52000.

tasks.prompt: In **B4**, type her joining date, **1 August 2026**, so Excel stores a real date.
hints: A real date lines up on the right.

tasks.prompt: In **B5**, type her employee ID **0042** so the zeros stay.
hints: Start the entry with an apostrophe.

mistakes.msg: Excel turned it into 42 and dropped the zeros. Type '0042 with an apostrophe first.

tasks.prompt: In **B6**, record that she has a laptop with the logical value **TRUE**.
hints: Logical values are TRUE or FALSE.
It will sit in the centre of the cell.

tasks.prompt: The claims in **D2:D5** arrived as text, so the total in D6 is 0. Turn them into real numbers.
hints: Look for the green triangles and left alignment.
Select D2:D5, right-click and choose Convert to number.
Or click each cell and retype the number.

quiz.q: Which entry will Excel store as text?
quiz.explain: An apostrophe at the start tells Excel to keep the entry as text.

quiz.q: Where does a number line up in a cell by default?
quiz.explain: Numbers and dates line up on the right; text on the left.

quiz.q: You type 0091 in a cell. What does Excel show?
quiz.explain: Leading zeros are dropped from numbers.

quiz.q: Why is a 16-digit card number unsafe as a number in Excel?
quiz.explain: The 16th digit becomes 0. Store long IDs as text.
Dates are day numbers with a date format on top.

points: Text sits left, numbers and dates right, TRUE/FALSE centre.
Keep IDs with leading zeros as text with an apostrophe: `'0042`.
Green triangles mean numbers stored as text: Convert to Number.
recap.cheat: Left means text. If a number or date sits on the left, Excel doesn’t see it as one.
